schools.summary: Gill reports the Targum's 'one language and one counsel' and takes exception to the middle term, granting the one language but denying the one counsel, since it does not appear all were of a mind about the city and the tower, and he thinks it unlikely Shem and his sons were in the design. Calvin refuses the guess that the tower was a refuge against a second flood, saying those who conjecture it have no guide but the dream of their own brain, since the words note nothing but mad ambition and proud contempt of God; what he finds in the text is the wish for a name, headstrong pride behind which he hears the fable of the giants heaping mountains to pull Jove from his throne, and he sets the date by Peleg against a fragment allowing only a hundred and thirty years from the flood, closing on Noah, wounded to the depth by such a counsel among his own posterity.

Henry sets the scene before the building: the families had been assigned their several ways after the flood, but men were loth to disperse, reckoning the more the merrier and the safer, and thought themselves wiser than either God or Noah; two things befriended the design, the common language, since men who understand one another are the likelier to love and help one another, and the plain, spacious enough to hold them and fruitful enough to keep them, though they never asked what room there would be once their numbers grew, from which he draws the moral that present conveniences often tempt men to neglect both duty and interest for the future. He meets the flood-refuge guess with a practical objection, that men with that in view would have built on a mountain.

Clarke has no doubt which language it was, taking it for Hebrew and resting the claim on the proper names of Scripture, and passes on the reckoning that the tongue served all the world until Peleg was born and the Hebrews alone thereafter until the captivity. Wesley repeats Henry's point that a common language kept men from parting.

Ellicott sets the chapter after the table of nations, which had carried the reader over the whole known world, and reads the narrative as doubling back to give the reason for that dispersion; he renders the opening literally as of one lip and of words one, meaning that pronunciation and vocabulary alike were the same, and adds a note of his own time that where the gulf between Sanscrit and the Semitic tongues was lately thought unbridgeable, recent inquiry tends to show a common basis under both.

themes: the whole earth was of one language
why men were loth to disperse
the plain of Shinar as a temptation
the date of Babel and the days of Peleg

2.pericope_label: The journey east and the making of brick

schools.summary: Gill reports the dispute over the opening phrase without settling it. Calvin turns the difficulty of the materials into an aggravation of the guilt, since men who had neither stone nor mortar to hand went to the labour of burning brick and gathering slime rather than let the work drop, and he quotes Horace on the audacity that will bear anything.

Clarke defends the rendering from the east from ordinary usage and describes the brick and the bitumen, the slime of the region serving in place of mortar. Wesley states the two aims of the builders, a name and the prevention of their dispersion, observes that history has not preserved one builder's name, and objects to the flood-refuge guess that men with that in view would have built on a mountain rather than a plain.

Ellicott argues for eastward against all the versions, and reports the cement found at the Birs-Nimroud as confirming the account of the materials. Keil and Delitzsch have the company move south-east into a broad plain.

debates.question: Does the phrase mean that they journeyed from the east, or eastward?

sides.position: from the east, as ordinary Hebrew usage requires

themes: from the east or eastward
brick for stone and slime for mortar
let us make us a name
the fear of being scattered abroad

schools.summary: Gill rejects the notion that the tower was meant as a refuge from another flood. Calvin finds the whole motive in the wish for a name: to erect a citadel was no great crime, but to raise a monument that should endure through all ages was headstrong pride; he cites David and Juvenal, remarks that more pride is often displayed at funerals than at weddings, and rejects both the reading that fixes on before we are scattered and the guesses that make the builders warned by Noah or unwitting prophets of their own dispersion.

Clarke reports two alternatives to the flood-refuge theory, Hutchinson's that the tower was a temple to the host of heaven with the one lip understood as one litany, and the Targums' that it carried a talisman image bearing a sword, and notes the later dedication of the place to Bel.

Ellicott reads the tower as a beacon and a means of centralisation, the builders meaning to hold mankind together at one seat, and doubts aloud whether centralisation promotes human happiness; he too rejects the flood-refuge guess.

debates.question: What was the tower built for?

sides.position: a refuge against a second flood — rejected by all who report it
a temple to the host of heaven, or a talisman bearing an image with a sword
a beacon and a centre, to keep mankind from separating
nothing but ambition for an enduring name

themes: a tower whose top may reach unto heaven
what the tower was for
let us make us a name
lest we be scattered abroad

schools.summary: Gill denies that the coming down was local or visible, God being immense, omnipresent and invisible, and denies too that it was to learn what he could not see from heaven, since he is omniscient; the phrase covers some display of power that made his presence plain, and he passes on the Targum's rendering that the Lord was revealed to take vengeance. He finds in the verse both patience and justice, God not proceeding at once and examining the truth of the matter before sentence. Calvin says the descent is spoken with reference to men rather than to God, who does not move from place to place, and explains the delay severely: God seemed for a little while to take no notice, so that by breaking the work off suddenly at its commencement he might give the more decisive evidence of his judgment, since he often bears with the wicked so far as to further their designs with animating success, that he may at length cast them down lower.

Henry makes it a rule that before God gave judgment upon their cause he enquired into it, for he condemns none unheard, and calls the coming down itself condescension, God humbling himself to behold the transactions of this lower world. He reads the children of men for three things, their frailty, since it was foolish in worms of the earth to defy heaven, their sin, the Hebrew reading sons of that disobedient Adam, and their separation from the children of God, pious Eber not being found among them. He gives the two grounds of the sentence, their oneness and their obstinacy, and draws from the first a rebuke, that unity is a policy but not the infallible mark of a true church.

Clarke has only a line, quoting an ancient Jewish commentator that this is a lesson to magistrates to examine every evidence before they decree judgment. Wesley abridges Henry on the three senses of the children of men.

themes: the Lord came down to see
spoken after the manner of men
God condemns none unheard
the children of men

6.pericope_label: The counsel to confound their language

schools.summary: Gill denies the words are addressed to angels, against Aben Ezra and the Targum, citing Philo that those addressed are treated as fellow workers, which no creature could be, since it is beyond any creature to work upon the mind and the faculty of speech; the words are the Father speaking to the Son and the Spirit. Calvin rejects the Jewish reading on the ground that no angels are mentioned and that God places those he addresses in the same rank with himself, takes the passage as answering to let us make man after our image, and thinks it not improperly adduced in proof that three Persons subsist in one essence. On the tone of the sixth verse he canvasses complaint and an argument from less to greater before settling on a suppressed irony, God setting himself the hard task of breaking a people welded into a firm conspiracy; in the seventh he has Moses paint the scene so that the judgment stands before the eye, God saying he will not use many instruments but will only blow upon them.

Clarke handles the opening particle, noting that go to now means nothing in English while the Hebrew carries come or make ready, and supposes the first language monosyllabic, each word bearing one meaning, so that the judgment was less the coining of new tongues than a change in how the same word was sounded and understood; he illustrates it from Du Bartas and adds that the tongues of the earth were not formed in a moment, climate and trade and government having their share, while Arabic, Syriac and Ethiopic still bear a likeness to their parent. Wesley notes the fitness of the means, since men who cannot understand one another can neither help nor enjoy one another, reckons the cost as continuing in every language we must learn, judges the scheme of a universal character a vain thing striving against a divine sentence, and closes at Pentecost.
Keil and Delitzsch treat these verses with the genealogy that follows and mark the paragraph as the close of the dispersion before the line returns to Shem.

themes: let us go down and confound their language
to whom does God speak?
what the confusion of tongues was
Babel and Pentecost

8.pericope_label: The scattering and the name of Babel

schools.summary: Gill states the irony that the very thing the builders feared came upon them by the measures they took to guard against it, and that those who shared a speech drew together and departed in bodies until the earth was peopled, as God had willed; he takes Babel for confusion, notes that Josephus says the Hebrews use the word so, guesses the sons of Eber may have fastened it on the place, and adds that Nimrod afterwards carried the work on and made the city the beginning of his kingdom, while heathen writers such as Eupolemus assign the scattering to a divine hand. Calvin insists on a distinction, that men had already been spread abroad by blessing and grace, whereas here those whom the Lord had distributed with honour he ignominiously scatters, driving them like the members of a lacerated body, not a simple dispersion for replenishing the earth but a violent rout; and he reads the name as the answer to their ambition, since they gain a name but not such a one as they would have chosen.

Clarke presses that God would not permit a single seat of government and made the means devised to prevent dispersion the instrument of accomplishing it, since humanly speaking the earth could not have been peopled so quickly otherwise; he derives the name from a root meaning to mingle or confound, repeats that the confusion lay in a new pronouncing of old words rather than in new tongues, and dismisses the story of seventy-two nations and languages as an idle and unfounded tale.

Ellicott describes the mechanism without further miracle, each tribe holding intercourse only with those of its own dialect, so that the divine purpose of occupying the world took effect while the project of an ambitious knot of men was frustrated; he works the philology out at length, taking Babel for Bab-el, the gate of God, refusing the derivation from the gate of Bel, and observing that man calls his city the gate of God while God calls it Babble, since confused speech is figured in every language by the lips producing that sound. He notes that the Babylonian legends agree in making the building impious and a Titanic attempt on heaven, and inclines to identify the tower with the observatory at Borsippa rather than the temple of Bel.

themes: the Lord scattered them abroad
they left off to build the city
the meaning of the name Babel
the Babylonian legends of the tower

10.pericope_label: The generations of Shem to Terah

schools.summary: Gill limits the list to the line that led to Abraham, by which the true descent of the Messiah from Adam might appear, and fills the interval with darker notices, that idolatry spread in Reu's days and that Terah was the first of this line to fall from the true religion. Calvin looks at what the chapter adds to the tenth, the term of each man's life, without which we should not know how much time lay between the deluge and the covenant with Abram, and reads the choice of this family for the world's calendar as a mark of honour, as historians date their annals by kings or consuls; he traces the narrowing of the election from Arphaxad to Selah to Eber and so to Abram, whose calling should be reckoned the renovation of the Church.

Henry calls this no endless genealogy, since it ends in Abram the friend of God and carries on to Christ, and reckons that twice ten and thrice fourteen descents lie between the first Adam and the second, establishing that Christ was son of Abraham, son of man and seed of the woman; he dwells on what the passage withholds, nothing being left on record but names and ages, the Holy Ghost seeming to hasten through them to the story of Abram, and draws from it that we know little of those gone before us and have enough to do to mind our own day's work. On the shortening of life he refuses any appeal to a decay of nature and imputes the change to the wise disposal of Providence, noting that Eber outlived all born after the flood, perhaps as the reward of his strict adherence to the ways of God.

Clarke calls the line the holy family and says plainly that scriptural chronology as it stands in the Hebrew, the Samaritan, the Greek, Josephus and some of the fathers is greatly embarrassed, sending his reader to Hales rather than arguing it out; he does settle the second Cainan, inserted by the Greek and followed by Luke but absent from the Hebrew here and in Chronicles, as a spurious generation, and explains that Abram is named first for dignity though Haran was the eldest, as Scripture sets Shem before his brothers and Moses before Aaron. Wesley follows Henry closely on the silence of the record and the shortening of men's lives.

themes: these are the generations of Shem
the gradual shortening of life
the embarrassment of scriptural chronology
Abram named first though not the eldest

schools.summary: Gill notes only how short the genealogy is, giving the three sons over again and no more. Calvin argues at length that Abram was not the firstborn: if he were born in Terah's seventieth year we must lose sixty years of Terah's life, which is absurd; he calls Luther's guess that God buried the time in oblivion to hide the end of the world frivolous, thinks the suggestion of a sixty-year stay at Charran most improbable, since there would be no end in protracting the journey's middle, and observes that Moses simply does not say in what year Terah begat his sons.

Henry opens the story of Abram with the country, Ur of the Chaldees, an idolatrous land where even the children of Eber had degenerated, and says those who are by grace heirs of the promise ought to remember the land of their nativity and the rock out of which they were hewn; he settles the birth order from the numbers, Terah dying at two hundred and five and Abram leaving Haran at seventy-five, so that Abram was born in his father's hundred and thirtieth year and was probably the youngest, adding that in God's choices the last are often first. He names the relations for Abram's sake, Terah who served other gods beyond the river, Nahor whose family supplied the wives of Isaac and Jacob, and Haran the father of Lot, and hangs on the halt at Charran the warning that many reach to Charran and yet fall short of Canaan.
Wesley reproduces Henry's reasoning on the birth order and on the family named for Abram's sake.

Ellicott marks this tôldôth as running to the eleventh verse of the twenty-fifth chapter and calls it one of the most interesting in Genesis, since God laid in Abraham the foundation of the intermediate dispensation and of the Jewish Church; he explains the heading by Terah's name as joining Abraham to the past and showing him the representative of Shem, and stands alone in defending Abram's birthright, holding that to deny him the first place for the sake of spiritual pre-eminence argues against the rules of the Hebrew language.

debates.question: Was Abram the eldest son of Terah?

sides.position: no; the numbers put his birth in Terah’s hundred and thirtieth year, and he is named first for dignity
yes; to deny him the birthright argues against the rules of the Hebrew language

themes: the generations of Terah
was Abram the firstborn?
Ur of the Chaldees an idolatrous land

28.pericope_label: Haran's death, the wives, and Sarai's barrenness

schools.summary: Gill takes the phrase for in his father's sight, with Jarchi and Aben Ezra, and says it marks the place more than the time; he supposes the surviving brothers married after Haran's death, taking his daughters, and on Sarai's barrenness records that Aben Ezra had heard the defect laid to Abram, which he calls the reverse of Scripture and refutes from Ishmael and the sons of Keturah. Calvin says only that Haran left his father the survivor and died in Ur, and spends his indignation on the Jewish tale, forged from the derivation of Ur from fire, that Haran and Abram were thrown into a furnace for refusing idolatry; Joshua's charge that the whole family served other gods disposes of it, and cities take their names from situation or event. On the barrenness he answers that the reason is given to show nothing short of a miracle brought Isaac, God meaning to humble his servant, who watched the wicked multiply while he alone was childless, and showing in him as in a mirror how the Church would arise, lying hid at that time like a dry root under the earth.
Clarke rejects the common view that Sarai and Iscah are one person under two names, since Iscah is expressly called Haran's daughter while Sarai was Terah's, and so Abram's half-sister.

Ellicott renders the phrase in the presence of his father and calls it the first recorded premature death by natural decay; he identifies Ur with the mounds of Mugheir, first held by Accadians and afterwards taken by Semites, follows Sayce in dating the consolidation of the Chaldean kingdoms under Lig-Bagas about three thousand years before Christ, and draws the consequence that Abraham left a famous seat of learning and may have carried its records with him, which accounts for the resemblance between the earlier chapters of Genesis and the cuneiform narratives — though he presses the unlikeness as hard, the inscriptions owning twelve superior gods and countless inferior ones while Chaldean literature has nothing so grand as the opening words of Genesis. On the wives he agrees with Clarke and disposes of Ewald's guess that Iscah was Lot's wife, noting that marriage between near relatives was allowed then but not between children of the same mother.

themes: Haran died before his father
Ur of the Chaldees and the cuneiform record
was Sarai the same as Iscah?
but Sarai was barren

31.pericope_label: The departure from Ur and the halt at Haran

schools.summary: Gill lingers over the careful naming of Lot and Sarai and finds it leaves us in the dark, giving Aben Ezra's difficulty that had Sarai been Terah's daughter the verse would have named her so; he observes that Terah's years are summed up as no one else's are here, his death being the moment Abram left Chaldea, reports an Arabic historian who gives Terah sixty years too many, and guesses that Terah named the place after his dead son. Calvin thinks the next chapter ought to begin here, since Moses turns to the calling of Abram and gives the journey's end as Canaan, from which he infers that Terah was the companion of his son rather than the leader; Abram had been called before he moved a foot from his native soil, and of Terah no call is recorded, so the oracle likely reached him by his son's report. From the arithmetic Calvin concludes that Terah left his country only a little before his death, since it is absurd that a man bound directly for Canaan should stay sixty years on the road.

Clarke describes Chaldea and Ur, whose site is not well known and whose name probably came from fire, the learned being nearly unanimous that its early inhabitants were fire-worshippers; he traces the Chaldees from Chesed, notes that those in Ur were priests or astronomers as well as idolaters and lent their name to astrologers ever after, and closes the chapter by counting its three great particulars, the building of Babel, the confusion of tongues and the call of Abram, with the three ends they served.

Ellicott notes that the phrase they went forth with them is strange and that a slight transposition gives the Samaritan, Greek and Latin reading, that Terah brought them forth; he identifies Haran with Carrhae in north-west Mesopotamia, distinguishes it from the name of Lot's father, and offers two motives for the migration, partly a northward drift of Semites made restless by the Elamites and chiefly a religious one, Ur being the especial seat of the moon-god. He adds that by the Samaritan text Abram left in the year his father died, Nahor having probably joined the household by then.

themes: they went forth to go into the land of Canaan
who led the migration, Terah or Abram?
Ur, the Chaldees, and the worship of fire
Terah died in Haran
